We sincerely thank all the reviewers for carefully reading our paper and providing thoughtful comments and suggestions. We are glad that the reviewers found our work timely (iDpM), our paper clear and well-written (iDpM, sRe5, FYjq), our framework novel (sRe5, 8wqF, FYjq), and our experimental results convincing (sRe5, 8wqF, FYjq). Our work proposes a principled and theoretically grounded RL fine-tuning method for dLLMs by matching the dLLM policy distribution to the reward-tilted target distribution through weighted denoising cross-entropy loss, which we believe will inspire future research in this direction.

The main concerns raised by the reviewers include:

1. Lack of ablation studies on SFT and hyperparameters (e.g., resampling frequency, number of rollouts) (iDpM, sRe5, FYjq);
2. Methodological questions regarding the WDCE loss (iDpM, sRe5).

In our rebuttal, we provide a comprehensive, point-to-point response to address the concerns raised by the reviewers. We have also updated our manuscript, where notable changes are highlighted in $\color{orange}{\rm orange}$. The main modifications to the paper are summarized as follows:

## (I) Enhanced experimental results

We took the reviewers' advice and incorporated the following new experimental results into the paper to further enhance its quality:

1. DMPO with post-trained model, LLaDA-SFT (LLaDA-Instruct 8B with SFT on a high quality reasoning dataset of 1k question-answer pairs) and LLaDA-1.5 (LLaDA-Instruct 8B with DPO on a diverse datasets of 350k preference pairs) (Tab. 1), which **continues to show significant performance gains**;
2. Coupled-GRPO baseline (Tab. 1) for providing a more comprehensive comparison;
3. Ablation studies on the hyperparameters (Figs. 7, 8 in App. C.3) to demonstrate the method's **robustness and effectiveness**;
4. Comparison of sample entropy between DMPO and diffu-GRPO (Fig. 9 in App. C.3) to demonstrate that WDCE loss (cross-entropy based method) is **less prone to mode seeking** and maintains a higher level of diversity;
5. **Improved performance of DMPO on several tasks and generation length** (Tab. 1).

## (II) Additional explanations and clarifications

We have added several paragraphs for additional discussions and explanations on the advantage of DMPO, with the following major changes:

1. We illustrate the considerable improvement of DMPO (compared with diffu-GRPO) in **sample and compute efficiency** due to being *forward* and *off-policy* in Sec. 4, Line 504 - Line 515. We conduct a series of controlled experiments on DMPO and diffu-GRPO, each ran with a fixed training budget to demonstrate the efficiency and efficacy of DMPO (Fig. 6). 
2. We elucidate the **instrinsic difference** between the off-policy learning in DMPO and that of diffu-GRPO, GRPO or PPO, in Sec. 4, Line 516 - Line 528. DMPO uses importance sampling with sequence-level importance sampling weights $\frac{p_*}{p_{\text{old}}}$, which is **independent of current model policy** $\pi_{\theta}$ and will not exhibits higher variances as training progresses. Instead, off-policy diffu-GRPO uses token-level importance sampling weights $\frac{\pi_{\theta}}{\pi_{\text{old}}}$, whose variances largely hinges on the level of deviation of current policy from the old one and inevitably diverges as the number of parameter updates increases. 



## (III) Stochastic optimal control (SOC) formulation of WDCE

To clarify the methodological questions on the WDCE loss, in App. B.1, we present our DMPO framework and WDCE loss from the perspective of SOC. In particular, we emphasize that minimizing the KL divergence between **sequence-level probabilities** $p _ * (\boldsymbol{\xi} _ 1)$ and $p _ \theta (\boldsymbol{\xi} _ 1)\approx\mathrm{e}^{-\mathcal{L} _ \theta(\boldsymbol{\xi} _ 1)}$ with ELBO approximation in the WDCE loss (11) can be interpreted as *precisely* minimizing the KL divergence between **path-level probabilities** $\mathbb{P}^ * (\boldsymbol{\xi})$ and $\mathbb{P}^\theta(\boldsymbol{\xi})$, where $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\boldsymbol{\xi} _ t) _ {t\in[0,1]}$ is the generation path of the dLLM parameterized by time $t$, and $\mathbb{P}^*$, $\mathbb{P}^\theta$ are the path measures of the continuous-time Markov chains. This SOC perspective provides an strong support of the theoretical validity of the ELBO in WDCE, emphasizing that this is a **principled approach** rather than a heuristic approximation.

---

We thank the reviewers again for their valuable feedback and look forward to any further comments or questions.

> The use of ELBO in DMPO

We thank the reviewer for mentioning this aspect. To clearly illustrate that the use of ELBO is a principled approach rather than an heuristic, we have included a new section in App. B.1 on how DMPO can be derived naturally from a stochastic optimal control (SOC) perspective of our method. This justifies the validity of using ELBO in the algorithm. In short, from the SOC perspective, the ELBO can be interpreted as the **trajectory-level** probability of the diffusion process. This is different from the token-level likelihood used in PPO/GRPO, which causes the mismatch issue. We have also included this discussion in the main text in Line 319-323.

> Mismatch in results table on d1 and missing baseline on coupled GRPO.

We appreciate the reviewer for pointing this out. We have clarified in the paper that the results reported are based on **our own reproduction**, which is slightly different from the results reported in the original paper despite we exactly follow their instructions. For the coupled GRPO baseline from the DiffuCoder paper (arXiv:2506.20639), we include our own reproduced result in the cGRPO-LLaDA row in the updated Tab. 1. 

> Ablation results with SFT

We agree with the reviewer that it is important to evaluate the effect of RL on already-post-trained models. In Tab. 1, we include two new row of results where DMPO is applied to: (i) LLaDA-SFT, obtained by performing SFT of LLaDA-Instruct on s1k dataset; (ii) LLaDA-1.5, the LLaDA model post-trained by performing DPO on 350K preference pairs of data. Our results show that DMPO continues to deliver performance gains for post-trained models, with consistent and significant accuracy improvements over base models, especially at generation lengths of $128$ and $256$ for the math reasoning datasets.

> Eq. 7 and partition function

We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. The difficulty of optimization does not arise from intractability of the partition function. What we meant here is that we don't have samples from $p _ *$, so we cannot directly compute the expectation over $p _ *$ with Monte Carlo. Instead, we use importance sampling with samples from $p _ v$.

> Explanation of small batch phenomena and negative gradient

We agree with the reviewer that modifying the importance weights changes the original distribution matching objective. However, as we have explained in Sec. 3.3, the original all-positive importance weights will be problematic under small batch sizes. This is due to that the policy distribution would be promoted to re-distribute more mass to **both good and bad** responses due to the positive weight they have, and remove mass from **unseen responses regardless of good or bad** to ensure the distribution is normalized to $1$. With the weight baseline subtraction and thus an insertion of negative gradient, we can properly reward good responses and penalize bad responses even in small batch sizes. 

To explain this more clearly, our method can be viewed as doing SFT (using the cross-entropy loss) on weighted samples generated by the model itself. After baseline subtraction, the signed weights signify the update direction for each sample, resembling the signed advantaged used in PPO/GRPO from a high level. Without it, when the batch size is small, as shown in Fig. 3 (b), the bad samples may dominate, leading to performance degradation.

> Baseline control variates results and variance control with clipping

We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. To illustrate that other proposed baseline are just as effective, we ran the new results updated in Tab 1 (DMPO-LLaDA-SFT, DMPO-LLaDA-1.5) with the individual weight baseline instead of the group weight baseline. The results clearly reflects the effectiveness of this method. 

As for other variance control techniques, the well-known techniques such as reward standardization and weight clipping are not directly feasible, as we explained below: 
- For reward standardization, as we are not in the reward maximization paradigm, it has little impact on our objective loss. Since we use softmax to compute the weights, the subtracted reward mean takes no effect and the std normalization is equivalent to the temperature $\alpha$. 
- For weight clipping, since our importance weight are of the form $p_{*} / p_{\text{old}}$ instead of $p_{\theta} / p_{\text{old}}$, it does not centers around $1$ until the optimality is reached. Therefore, common clipping practice with $\operatorname{clip}(x, 1-\epsilon, 1+ \epsilon)$ does not help stabilizing the training in DMPO.

Due to these difficulties and infeasibility of existing techniques, we seek to develop **novel techniques** such as weight baseline subtraction to aid the training. We believe that this is a notable contribution to the general LLM post-training field by itself and can be applied to other scenarios as well.

We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments. We are glad that the reviewer found our paper novel and insightful, with convincing empirical results. Below we carefully address the concerns you raised in a point-by-point manner. 

---

> Clarify whether the issue is with reverse KL as optimization dynamics versus as objective definition

We appreciate the reviewer for allowing us to further clarify this point. The issue with reverse KL does not arise from its ground-truth, reward-tilted policy distribution. It rather came from the situation where we perform learning with data-approximated reverse KL divergence in practice and end up with imperfectly learnt policy distribution. 

When we achieve small loss value of reverse KL $\mathbb{E} _ {\pi _ {\theta}} (\log \pi _ {\theta} - \log \pi _ { * })\approx \epsilon$, $\pi _ {\theta}$ will closely matches the magnitude of $\pi _ { * }$ on the mode it already discovered in order to avoid large penalization from $\log \frac{\pi _ {\theta}}{\pi _ { * }}$, leading to the so-called **mode-seeking** behavior, neglecting the diversity of the response. 

On the other hand, when optimizing the forward KL divergence to have small loss value $\mathbb{E} _ {\pi _ { * }} (\log \pi _ { * } - \log \pi _ {\theta}) \approx \epsilon$, $\pi _ {\theta}$ would share a similar support as $\pi _ { * }$ (therefore avoiding to have large penalty from $-\log \pi _ {\theta}$ on $\boldsymbol{o}$ where $\pi _ {\theta}(\boldsymbol{o}) \approx 0$ but $\pi _ { * }(\boldsymbol{o}) \gg 0$), leading to the more desirable, diversity encouraged **mode-covering** phenomenon. 


> Stability of DMPO under small value for number of rollouts generated per prompt $N$

We agree with the reviewer that a small value for the number of rollouts generated per prompt $N$ may lead to a relatively high variance in theory. In practice, we found that performance of DMPO is rather robust to the value of $N$. We conduct an additional ablation study on the choice of this hyperparameter, and in Fig. 7 of App. C.3, we presented the performance of DMPO on Countdown with $N$ varying from $4$ to $32$. It can be seen that DMPO is **highly robust to the choice of $N$** as it works equally well under a wide range of values for $N$, with no additional computational overhead or performance degradation. We believe that the stability of DMPO to $N$ possibly originates from the following 3 aspects:
1. DMPO uses *sequence-level* importance weight rather than *token-level* ones used in GRPO, which have similarly been found to have better stability in GSPO [1].
2. DMPO uses importance weights computed from softmax operation, with a natural range in $(0,1)$, therefore having limited variance.
3. DMPO uses weight baseline subtraction to insert negative gradients. While this operation introduces a little bias into the objective, we believe that it help adjust the most important information among these weights: their **sign** and **relative magnitude**. It helps to properly classify good and bad responses, which alleviates the weight variance issue to some extent. 


> Application to AR-LLM and uniqueness of DMPO to dLLM

We highly appreciate the reviewer for pointing out this interesting direction. To the best of our knowledge, there is no prior work at the time of the submission that applies cross entropy like our method to RL for AR LLMs, which signifies the novelty of our proposed approach.  The closest approach in AR-LLM is FlowRL [2] (concurrent to our work), which studies distribution matching for AR-LLM, but only utilized GFlowNet objective derived from reverse KL to achieve the goal. This has also been thoroughly discussed in the related work section in Line 1030-1032.

What is unique of DMPO to diffusion LLM lies in the stochastic optimal control (SOC) characterization of the method, which makes **the application to dLLM more natural than AR-LLM**. In App. B.1, we newly include a derivation of the WDCE loss and DMPO from the perspective of performing SOC of continuous-time markov chain (CTMC) on the space of path measures. This characterization perfectly aligns with diffusion LLM, which is driven by discrete diffusion models and described also through CTMC. This perfect match promotes us to first consider application to dLLM instead of AR-LLM. However, we also agree with the reviewer that DMPO can be easily extended to AR-LLM, and this is an exciting direction to explore as future works.

> Clarification on masking in d1

Thanks for pointing out the mistake. We have corrected it in the updated version in Line 155-156

We thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback. We are glad that the reviewer finds our paper clear, well-structured, and with strong empirical results. Below we carefully address the concerns you raised in a point-by-point manner. 

> Limited model generality

We thank the reviewer for pointing out this limitation of our work. We agree that it is important to evaluate our method on a wider range of dLLM structures, and we have already mentioned this limitation in Sec. 5 (conclusion). The scope of this work is to introduce the novel DMPO framework for dLLMs, and we believe that the methodology can be adapted to other dLLM architectures with minor modifications. Our experiments on the LLaDA-8B family serve as a proof of concept and a comparison with existing methods. Also, LLaDA-8B is one of the best open-source models at the time this work is submitted, and is widely adopted in many studies in dLLMs. 

To ease the concern of generalization of DMPO to other base models, we have included additional results on LLaDA-SFT and LLaDA-1.5, two new base models with stronger performances than LLaDA-Instruct-8B, and reported the results in Tab. 1. The results shown that DMPO manage to gain consistent performance increases over these new base models, confirming the generality of the approach.

For the exploration on larger, more competent dLLMs, we agree with the reviewer that this is an important next step, and we will save it for future investigation.

> Training compute efficiency characterization of DMPO

We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion to better showcase the advantage of our method. We took your advice and conduct additional comparison with diffu-GRPO, a SOTA dLLM RL method, and reported the results in Fig. 6. Thanks to the off-policy and forward nature of the method, DMPO can achieves similar reward learning performances as diffu-GRPO with as less as $31\\%$ of the training compute used quantified through PF-days. This emphasizes the great improvement in training efficiency brought up by DMPO. We have included a more thorough discussion in Sec. 4, Line 504-529.

---

We hope that our responses adequately address the reviewer's concerns. We are committed to improving our work and appreciate the valuable feedback provided.

We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments. We are glad that the reviewer found our paper novel with satisfatory empirical performances.

For the sequence length used in the MATH500 experiments, we choose $128, 256, 512$ to align with our baseline method d1, which considers the same sequence length setting. We certainly agree with the reviewer that for complex reasoning tasks like MATH500, a longer response length may be beneficial for better performances. However, diffusion LLM like LLaDA are mostly encoder-only, whose computation is costly and memory-inefficient without appropriate KV caching mechanism activated, compared to their decoder-only AR LLM counterparts. This creates an extra layer of difficulty when we attempt to scaling DMPO to longer response lengths. Due to these computational-wise concerns, we do not explore generation length beyond $512$ in this work, and we will save it for future explorations.

---

We thank the reviewer again for the insightful comments. If any part of our response or the manuscript is unclear, please feel free to raise your concerns, and we will happily provide more details and clarifications.

summary.value: This paper proposes a novel reinforcement learning algorithm for finetuning diffusion large language models (dLLMs) for reasoning tasks based on distribution matching.

reviewer_concerns.value: The most major concerns are (1) the limited novelty, with distribution matching being a widely used technique, and (2) the limited scope of the empirical evaluation, with most of the gains coming from two simple reasoning tasks. There were also a number of more low-level concerns, which largely stem from a variety of design choices that the authors made that were not sufficiently justified either from a theoretical or empirical perspective. While the authors made some progress towards addressing these lower-level concerns, the more major concerns persist.

reviewer_scores.value: I believe the major concerns regarding the scope of the contributions, both theoretical and empirical, was not sufficiently address, so the reviewers were unlikely to have updated their scores.

summary.value: This paper presents Distribution Matching Policy Optimization (DMPO), a novel reinforcement learning framework for enhancing reasoning in diffusion LLMs (dLLMs). Instead of maximizing rewards, DMPO matches the model's policy distribution to an optimal, reward-tilted target distribution. This is achieved using a Weighted Denoising Cross-Entropy (WDCE) loss, which enables efficient off-policy training by leveraging the dLLM's forward noising process. A novel weight baseline subtraction technique is introduced for training stability. On multiple reasoning benchmarks, DMPO achieves state-of-the-art results, significantly outperforming baselines without supervised fine-tuning, validating its distribution-matching approach.

strengths.value:
1. The paper presents clear, well-structured reasoning that connects diffusion LLM characteristics to the choice of forward KL (cross-entropy) objectives, with intuitive illustrations (e.g., mode-seeking vs mass-covering in Figure 2) and algorithmic clarity in Algorithm 1.
2. The empirical results show strong and consistent gains across diverse reasoning tasks (GSM8K, MATH500, Countdown, Sudoku) and multiple generation lengths, with particularly large improvements on planning-style benchmarks (e.g., +18% over d1 on Countdown and +11.8% on Sudoku), supporting the method’s effectiveness.
3. The experimental setup is carefully controlled and transparent, comparing against competitive dLLM baselines, reproducing d1 with recommended settings, and reporting training dynamics (Figure 4) and ablations (Figure 5), which strengthens the credibility of the findings.

weaknesses.value:
1. Limited model generality: The study evaluates DMPO exclusively on the LLaDA-8B family, leaving its applicability to other diffusion LLM , which constrains claims of broader generalization.

2. Incomplete efficiency characterization: Although the method emphasizes forward-only, off-policy training as an efficiency advantage, the paper lacks comprehensive, end-to-end comparisons (throughput, latency, memory footprint, and wall-clock cost) against strong baselines like diffu-GRPO or AR-LLM RL, making the practical scalability gains insufficiently quantified.

questions.value:
1. Does DMPO generalize beyond LLaDA (to other dLLM architectures/sizes) without extensive retuning?
2. Can you provide end-to-end efficiency metrics (throughput, latency, memory, wall-clock) versus diffu-GRPO and AR-LLM RL?

title.value: Rebuttal Overview -- Key Contributions, Concerns, Responses, and Updates

comment.value:
We thank all reviewers again for their valuable feedback and constructive comments, and we also thank PCs, SACs, and ACs for their time and effort in managing the review process amid the OpenReview system issues during the rebuttal period. As the reviewers cannot engage in further discussions at this stage, we summarize the main points of our rebuttal here for clarity for the ACs, in the hope that it will help with the final decision.

### **Contribution and Novelty of our Work**

Our paper studies the reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning of diffusion large language models (dLLMs) for enhancing their reasoning capabilities, a timely and important problem given the recent surge of interest in dLLMs. Our main contributions and novelties are as follows:

- **New learning framework**: We proposed a novel RL framework for dLLMs that targets **distribution matching** rather than reward maximization: matching the dLLM output distribution $p _ \theta(\boldsymbol{o}|\boldsymbol{q})$ to the reward-tilted target distribution $p _ * (\boldsymbol{o}|\boldsymbol{q})\propto p _ \text{base}(\boldsymbol{o}|\boldsymbol{q})\mathrm{e}^{r(\boldsymbol{o},\boldsymbol{q})/\alpha}$, instead of maximizing expected reward on output $\mathbb{E} _ {\boldsymbol{q}}\mathbb{E} _ {p _ \theta(\boldsymbol{o}|\boldsymbol{q})}[r(\boldsymbol{o},\boldsymbol{q})]$ as in prior works such as PPO and GRPO, which may suffer from reward hacking (Sec. 3.1)
- **Novel training objective**: Inspired by stochastic optimal control, we instantiated this framework with a novel training objective based on forward KL divergence, namely the **weighted denoising cross-entropy (WDCE)** loss. WDCE is ***off-policy*** and ***forward*** in nature and better aligns with the generation process of dLLMs, leading to superior sample and compute efficiency compared with existing on-policy methods (Sec. 3.2).
- **Tackling a special challenge**: We identified a special challenge that occurred for WDCE due to **small batch sizes**, and proposed **weight baseline subtraction** and **weighted direct discriminative optimization** to address it (Secs. 3.3 and 3.4).
- **Superior empirical performance**: We conducted extensive experiments on multiple reasoning tasks, demonstrating that our method not only significantly outperforms SOTA dLLM RL methods such as diffu-GRPO and coupled-GRPO, but also enjoys significant speedups with approximate KV-cache and outstanding training stability with stale data (Sec. 4).

Overall, we believe that our work makes significant contributions to the field of RL fine-tuning for dLLMs, and is to inspire future research in this direction.

### **Main Concerns Raised by Reviewers and Our Responses**

We are grateful to the reviewers for their careful reading and constructive comments. Below, we summarize the representative concerns raised by the reviewers, and briefly outline our responses. Detailed point-to-point responses are provided in individual responses to each reviewer.

#### **Ablation Studies and Critical Evidence to Several Claims**

The reviewers asked for

1. Empirical results of DMPO's performance on models with SFT (iDpM);
2. The hyperparameter sensitivity of DMPO (e.g., resampling frequency, number of rollouts), and how they improve performance (iDpM, sRe5);
3. Evidence of the claimed benefit of cross-entropy loss for diversity maintenance (iDpM, sRe5).

In our rebuttal, we have incorporated the following explanations and new experimental results into the paper to address these concerns:

1. We evaluated DMPO on two **post-trained LLaDA-8B models**: LLaDA-SFT and LLaDA-1.5 in Tab. 1, which shows that DMPO **continues to deliver significant performance gains for post-trained models**.
2. We conducted **ablation studies** on the number of rollouts per prompt $N$ in Fig. 7 and the resampling frequency $F$ in Fig. 8, showing DMPO is robust to $N$ while benefiting from $F$ as large as $24$, highlighting **the advantage of off-policy and forward nature** of DMPO.
3. We plot the **entropy curves** of DMPO and diffu-GRPO during training in Fig. 9, in which DMPO consistently produces higher entropy rollouts, validating our claim that WDCE is **less prone to mode seeking**.

summary.value: This paper introduces the DMPO algorithm, an RL algorithm designed for reasoning dLLMs training that treats policy optimization as a distribution matching procedure. The algorithm employs a novel objective function, WDCE, an off-policy forward loss that can leverage the inference acceleration techniques of dLLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that models trained with DMPO achieve SOTA performance on math and puzzle tasks without requiring SFT.

strengths.value:
1. The method is not merely a policy optimization algorithm for AR-LLMs. It proposes an RL modeling framework tailored for dLLMs.
2. The proposed loss function is computationally aligned with dLLM inference mechanisms and off-policy RL algorithm.
3. The approach achieves strong results across multiple reasoning tasks.

weaknesses.value: 1.The sequence length appears to be somewhat short. E.g. problems in MATH500 may require up to around 2048 tokens. It is unclear why the authors imposed such a limitation on reasoning length; testing with longer sequences may be worth considering.

questions.value: Please consider addressing the issue raised in the weakness section.

comment.value:
#### **Methodological Questions Regarding the WDCE Loss**

The reviewers ask us to

1. Clarify the purpose of weight baseline subtraction under small batch sizes (iDpM);
2. Clarify whether the disadvantage with reverse KL is as optimization dynamics or objective definition (sRe5);
3. Justify the validity of ELBO approximation (iDpM);
4. Discuss if our method can be extended to AR-LLMs (sRe5).

In response,

1. We clarified that weight baseline subtraction is critical for stabilizing training under small batch sizes by ensuring that both **good and bad** samples are properly **rewarded and penalized**, respectively.
2. We clarified that the issue with reverse KL is not with its optimal distribution $p _ *$, but rather when we use it as the **training objective**, which leads to **mode-seeking** behavior.
3. We included a new section in App. B.1 on the **stochastic optimal control (SOC)** perspective of our method. Through this lens, the ELBO approximation on the **sequence-level** probability can be interpreted as the exact **trajectory-level** probability of the diffusion process.
4. We believe our general framework of distribution matching policy optimization can be extended to AR-LLMs and continuous diffusion / flow-based models as well, and we have included a discussion on this in App. A.

### **Improvements of the Paper during Rebuttal**

In addition to our response to the reviewers' comments, we have also made significant improvements to the paper during the rebuttal period. Please refer to the general response part below for detailed explanations, and check our updated manuscript where notable changes are highlighted in $\color{orange}{\rm orange}$.

### **Concluding Remarks**

We thank the reviewers and ACs again for their time and effort in reviewing our paper and managing the review process. We hope that our responses and improvements during the rebuttal period have adequately addressed the reviewers' concerns. We will continue to improve the paper based on the valuable feedback received.

summary.value: This paper is motivated by criticizing the reverse KL objective's mode-seeking behavior, which might result in diversity collapse and reward hacking. They derive a distribution matching objective that learns to match the closed-form optimal distribution (originally derived as the solution to the reverse KL problem). They design a method DMPO to match this distribution using forward KL minimization via weighted cross-entropy with importance sampling. Their importance sampling approach removes the need to be on-policy, enabling replay buffer reuse. They provide multiple design choices for the weight baseline that gets subtracted from the importance weights.

strengths.value:
1. This paper provides a principled theoretical framework with clear derivations of the weighted denoising cross-entropy loss through importance sampling. The writing is clear and it is a good attempt to apply distribution matching for policy optimization for LLMs.
2. Their method enables off-policy training because their derived importance weights don't depend on the current policy, allowing replay buffer reuse for potential improved sample efficiency.
3. They shows consistent empirical improvements across multiple reasoning benchmarks.
4. They also identify and address the small batch size training challenge through novel weight baseline subtraction techniques with multiple design choices. The f-divergence and base-weight ablations are novel and insightful.

weaknesses.value:
1. The paper criticizes reverse KL for being mode-seeking and causing reward hacking, but it derives the target distribution p* as the solution to a reverse KL problem, then uses forward KL to match this p*. The paper should clarify whether the issue is with reverse KL as optimization dynamics versus as objective definition.
3. Regarding the stability of the proposed method: The partition function is estimated with only N=16 samples per prompt, which might create high variance in importance weights, especially when reward exponentials vary widely. Weight baseline subtraction adds another approximation layer on top of already noisy normalized weights. 
7. It seems this method could also be applied to autoregressive LLMs. Has any prior work in autoregressive LLM policy optimization done similar distribution matching work (this seems to be missing from related works)? And what's the uniqueness of applying this method for diffusion LLMs, given that the marginalization over orders and masking patterns creates more layers of variance on top of the importance ratio approximation?
4. Line 151 says d1 "fully masks all response positions except d" to estimate per-token probabilities. According to d1's Figure 2, it masks all response positions without exception in a single forward pass.
5. One main strength of this paper is that importance weights don't depend on the current policy, enabling replay buffer reuse for sample efficiency. However, the authors don't provide experiments demonstrating this sample efficiency with versus without replay (on-policy methods).
6. This work is motivated by improving diversity using forward KL. Can you share the entropy curves during RL to validate whether forward KL actually achieves its theoretical goal of maintaining diversity.

questions.value:
please see weakness.

How sensitives is this method wrt to hyperparameters like buffer sampling frequency F, number of rollouts N. Guidance on which are critical would be helpful.

comment.value:
> Gains mainly from sudoku and countdown

We thank the reviewer for the insightful question. We believe that this is due to the foundamental limit of the LLaDA-8B base model itself, which has a limited potential in solving complex reasoning tasks. Therefore, even with RL fine-tuning, the performance gain is limited. However, for simpler planning tasks like sudoku and countdown, the model can benefit more from RL fine-tuning. We also agree that it is an important future direction to explore the performance of our method on larger, more powerful dLLMs.

-----

We thank the reviewer again for the detailed review and valuable suggestions. If our responses and revisions have adequately addressed the raised concerns, we respectfully ask that the reviewer consider updating the rating accordingly. We are happy to provide additional explanations and revisions to further improve the paper and address any remaining concerns.

**Reference**: [1] Zheng et al. Group sequence policy optimization. arXiv:2507.18071.

We thank the reviewer for careful reading and valuable comments. We are glad that the reviewer finds our paper addresses an important and timely problem. Below we carefully addressed the concerns and questions in a point-by-point manner.

> Distribution Matching idea proposed in DMPO already identified in previous works. 

We thank the reviewer for mentioning the references and we have included them in the related work section in App. A. We agree that the idea of matching policy distribution to the reward-tilted one has been considered in the literature through minimizing functional $\mathcal{F}$ between probability measures is not new, as it reduces to the usual entropy-regularized reward optimization problem when $\mathcal{F}$ is specified to be the reverse KL divergence (also discussed in Line 198-201). 

However, we still present this policy distribution matching learning (Eq. 6) as we believe that it's a **principled framework** to derive new RL algorithms for fine-tuning. To the best of our knowledge, none of these works have proposed to use forward KL (weighted denoising cross entropy, WDCE) for dLLM fine-tuning. Moreover, we provide additional novel instantiations of this framework based on weighted direct discriminative optimization (WDDO) loss, which is also not explored in previous works. With the policy distribution matching framework, WDCE and WDDO can be naturally derived in an unified way by considering different instantiations of the functional $\mathcal{F}$, and we believe that this shows the reader a clearer reflection of our insights and motivation on this problem. 


> DMPO claims to avoid mode collapses and encourage diversity but no analysis or certificate of this claim. 

We thank the reviewer for raising this question. Our illustration of bi-modal Gaussian VI example in Fig. 2 might have created some confusion. Our arguments are not that LLM doesn't have enough capacity to fit the training data, and therefore having mode-covering behavior when optimized with forward KL. Our real claims are that LLM policy distribution are **prone to be more mode-covering** when optimized with forward KL in practice, therefore enjoying a better output diversity.

In practice, the objective are approximated with empirical data, and it's impossible to achieve the true ground truth (the reward-tilted distribution) even if the LLM has infinite capacity. Therefore, we pay attention to the behavior of the policy $\pi _ {\theta}$ when the loss objective is decently small (but not zero). When the forward KL $\mathbb{E} _ {\pi _ { * }}  (\log \pi _ { * } - \log \pi _ {\theta})$ is small enough, $\pi _ {\theta}$ would share a similar support as $\pi _ { * }$ (therefore avoiding to have large penalty from $-\log \pi _ {\theta}$ on $\boldsymbol{o}$ where $\pi _ {\theta}(\boldsymbol{o}) \approx 0$ but $\pi _ { * }(\boldsymbol{o}) \gg0$), leading to the mode-covering phenomenon.

To empirically validate the diversity improvement enjoyed by DMPO, we carry out additional analysis on the entropy of DMPO, in App. C.3, Fig. 9. Compared with diffu-GRPO, DMPO consistently produces higher entropy rollouts through the training, aligning with our expectation that DMPO has better output diversity. We hope that this additional experiment can serve as a concrete support of our initial claim in the paper.

> The advantage of off-policy in DMPO compared with GRPO/PPO

We appreciate the reviewer's question. This confusion raised potentially due to our initially insufficient discussion of the two major differences in importance sampling (IS) used in DMPO compared with that in GRPO/PPO. We have now added **additional explanations to clarify this aspect in Sec. 4, Line 516-528**. The two primary differences are (1) IS weight in DMPO is **independent** of current policy $\pi_{\theta}$, therefore will not diverge even if $\pi_{\theta}$ is heavily updated and diverge from $\pi_{\text{old}}$, while GRPO/PPO uses IS weight $\pi_{\theta}/\pi_{\text{old}}$ that would inevitably diverges as training progresses. (2) DMPO uses *sequence-level* IS weight that enjoys an additional layer of stability (also discussed in GSPO [1]) where *token-level* IS weight in GRPO/PPO does not enjoy. These combined enables DMPO to use highly stale data during training without suffering from collapses or instability. We also demonstrate in Fig. 8 that DMPO can uses **up to 24 updates per buffer** without sacrificing performances, leading to excellent sample and compute efficiency due to off-policy learning.

> Ablation studies on hyperameters and sample/compute efficiency of DMPO

We thank the reviewer for the great suggestion. In response, we have conducted additional ablation studies on the choice of rollouts number per prompt $N$ (in Fig. 7, App. C.3) and resampling frequency $F$ (in Fig. 8, App. C.3). We found that DMPO is high robust to both hyperparameter choice, with a significantly increased sample efficiency when using a large $F$. Compared with on-policy setting ($F = 1$), off-policy setting with $F > 1$ faciliates a more effective reward learning under the same compute budget. 

To further illustrate the advantage of DMPO in sample/compute efficiency, we also compare it to diffu-GRPO (our baseline method for performing RL on dLLM) and present the comparison in Fig. 6. From the curve, we can see that DMPO requires as less as $31\\%$ of the compute (quantified in PF-days) to achieve the same learning performance as diffu-GRPO, continuing to underscores the efficiency benefits. We also include a detailed discussion on this newly-added experiments in Sec. 4, Line 504-515. 

> Sample entropy of DMPO

We thank the reviewer for the suggestion. We have included the entropy curve in Fig. 9 at App. C.3. From the curve, it's clear that DMPO (based on forward-KL minimization) shows higher entropy compared with diffu-GRPO (based on reverse KL minimization), well certificating our theoretical claims on the sample diversity. 

---

We appreciate the reviewer's constructive feedback once again, which has helped us improve the clarity and quality of our work. We hope the above responses address the reviewer's concerns. We are happy to provide further clarifications if needed.

summary.value: This paper proposes a new method for post-training/fine-tuning of diffusion based LLMs (dLLMs). The authors argue that existing RLHF methods, which were originally proposed for  autoregressive LLMs, are suboptimal for dLLMs. They argue this because of mismatch between likelihood of generation and that used in RL. The main idea is to shift from reward maximization to the boltzmann distribution, a classic result knwon for entropy-regularized RL objectives. The method employs a reweighted denoising loss, by using importance weighting. Another proposed contribution is addressing a "small batch size" challenge, where they propose different forms of control variates. The paper shows performance gains over prior dLLM RL methods on reasoning benchmarks.

strengths.value: The paper's core premise is timely, as more research is being put into dLLMs. Applying RL to dLLMs, is a challenging and interesting problem. I do not see major theoretical flaws in the core argument. The small batch size problem that was considered is potentially interesting. The overall description is clear enough for someone to try replicating without much issue.

weaknesses.value:
Other papers have already identified the 'boltzmann distribution' matching idea. While that theoretical result is atleast a decade old (Ziebert et al), its application to dLLM is also known [1, 2].
This paper proposes KL minimization as objective, compared to the aforementioned works. 
The paper also claims DMPO avoids mode collapse and encourages diversity. While that makes sense from a high-level nature of the optimization objective; this also just assumes that the model cannot fit the data (which is unlikely for LLMs). Additionally, no analysis of these claims is presented. A similar concern arises from the 'off-policy' claim. Finally, even with methods like PPO, off-policy buffers get used regularly, so I do not see the specific possibilities arising from the proposed method. Finally, while the paper claims the PPO/GRPO objective is not principled due to mismatch between generation and used likelihood, that still applies here because of the ELBO. 

A last small issue is that I am not sure of the results table. While the numbers are broadly in line with what is reported in d1, they still differ significantly from reported results. Another missing baseline is [3]

[1] wd1: Weighted Policy Optimization for Reasoning in Diffusion Language Models
[2] PADRE: Pseudo-Likelihood based Alignment of Diffusion Language Models
[3] DiffuCoder: Understanding and Improving Masked Diffusion Models for Code Generation

questions.value:
I would like to see an ablation with SFT. While that may be important for boosting d1's result, it would be good to evaluate the proposed method with and without SFT.


In line 232, its written that Eq 7 is not amenable to optimization due to the partition function of p*. But that is irrelevant for optimization. Infact that is exactly what happens in Eq 9. 

While I can understand the criteria of variance reduction, I do not think that is not what is happening here. By changing the importance weighting, the whole idea of this being a distribution matching loss becomes untenable. I would also like a more detailed explanation of the small batch phenomena mentioned. It should be irrelevant with infinite data and perfect optimization. So it seems to me that the authors are claiming something else is happening, but I did not understand the explanation.


The final best subtractive weight is perhaps the simplest one. And the results shown there are also for the reward learning problem. I would like to see those baseline control variates in terms of actual results as well. I am also surprised that this weight reduction could not be achieved by clipping weights or reward standardization.

Most of the gains come from sudoku and/or countdown. Is there something specific in these tasks that make the proposed method better than GRPO etc.
